overview: The destroy packet removes entity ids from the client's world, and server-side anticheats mirror that removal in their entity trackers. Because reach and hitbox checks must never measure against an entity the client no longer sees, destroy handling is data hygiene: Kauri removes fake-mob state on the confirming keepalive, intave decodes the destroy payload across three protocol layouts, and Hydro deletes the tracked entity on the send side. The packet is never flagged; keeping the tracker in sync with it is what keeps entity checks honest.

checks.name: Destroy handling (Kauri)
checks.purpose: Remove fake-mob state for destroyed entities on the keepalive that confirms the destroy packet reached the client.
checks.how_it_works: PacketHandler routes DESTROY_ENTITIES (both modern and legacy wrappers) to EntityTrackHandler.onEntityDestroy, which schedules a keepalive action: for each destroyed id it calls removeFakeMob, despawning any fake mobs the anticheat placed next to the tracked entity and clearing the client-has-entity flag. Fake mobs are the anti-hitbox probes Kauri spawns around combat entities, so their lifecycle must mirror real despawns exactly or reach checks would measure against ghosts.
checks.detects: Nothing directly; the removal prevents ghost-entity false flags in the hitbox-based reach checks that use fake mobs.
checks.variations: Grim schedules entity removal on the destroy transaction and also clears serverPositionsMap and dashable and firework state; Tecnio and Hydro just remove the ids from their tracker maps; Artemis ReachPreProcessor drops the entity from reach tracking on the same packet.

checks.name: Destroy reader (intave)
checks.purpose: Decode the destroy payload across all protocol layouts and feed each entity id to the entity tracker.
checks.how_it_works: EntityDestroyReader implements EntityIterable over the destroy packet. It branches on protocol era: an int list on 1.17.1+, a single int on 1.17.0, and an int array on 1.16 and below, exposing both forEach and a substitution iterator so the tracker can read or rewrite ids. PacketReaders registers it under ENTITY_DESTROY, and EntityTracker.receiveEntityDestroy processes each id, dismounting riders and marking destroyed entities so AttackRaytrace can ignore them.
checks.detects: Nothing directly; the reader is the decode layer. The tracker's destroyed-entity marker (Entity.Destroyed) is what lets hitbox checks ignore dead entities.
checks.variations: Grim and Hydro wrap WrapperPlayServerDestroyEntities directly; FlopAC's WrappedOutEntityDestroy is the same idea on its tinyprotocol reflection layer.

checks.name: Destroy tracking (Hydro)
checks.purpose: Remove destroyed entities from the tracked-entity map so reach and entity queries never see despawned ids.
checks.how_it_works: EntityTracker.registerOutgoingPreHandler routes DESTROY_ENTITIES to handleDestroyEntities, which wraps WrapperPlayServerDestroyEntities and removes each id from the concurrent entityMap. Because insertion happens on spawn and removal on destroy, the map always mirrors the client's visible entity set; getDistanceToEntity and getClosestEntity simply cannot return a destroyed entity.
checks.detects: Nothing directly; it is the cleanup half of the tracker. Without it, reach checks would measure against entities the client no longer renders, producing false flags.
checks.variations: Tecnio removes ids from trackerMap on GPacketPlayServerEntityDestroy; Shard ejects riders before removing ids; Kauri defers cleanup to the confirming keepalive; TruthfulAC marks the entity destroyed with a grace window instead of deleting it outright.
